_comment: Copy to config.json and edit. config.json is gitignored: it holds the
camera's address, and on the ESP32 it will hold a hostname on the LAN.
rois starts empty on purpose. Aim the camera, open /roi, drag ONE box over
the whole row of drums, press 'Split selection into 8', then paste the
result here. Coordinates are pixels in the full sensor frame (2592x1944 on
the Mi A1), not in whatever the browser scaled it to.
Present because the camera pushes now. It wakes, shoots, sends and
sleeps, so there is no poll left to hand a verdict back to -- which
means this service has to fetch the previous reading and write the new
one itself. Under the pull model Home Assistant passed the prevalue in
and made the decision, and this block did not exist.
WHAT DID NOT CHANGE: whether a reading is good enough to keep is still
decided by gate(), in this repo, in code with tests. ha_publish() is
called only for a reading that already passed it. The token moved the
WRITING here, not the JUDGING.
LEAVE token EMPTY and put it in METERCAM_HA_TOKEN instead. This file is
readable from the ROI editor's own directory and gets pasted into
issues; a long-lived token that can drive the house does not belong in
it. The field is a fallback for a bench run, and the environment wins.
Drop the whole block and nothing breaks: /read then behaves exactly as
it always did -- prevalue comes from the query string, the verdict goes
back in the response, and Home Assistant decides. That is still the
right shape for anything that can poll.
prevalue_entity and write_entity are the same helper here, and that is
not an accident: it is the one the house has always typed into, and
everything downstream of it -- sensor.gas_meter_reading, both utility
meters, the Energy dashboard -- keeps working untouched.
Itron Gallus 2000 G4, serial U06000650, made 2011.
Qmax 6 m3/h, Qmin 0.04, Pmax 0.5 bar, V 1.2 dm3.
Index: 8 drums behind a glass window, reading to 0.001 m3. As of the
reference photo it stood at 02246.916.
POLARITY, which is worth knowing before blaming the model: this meter
is WHITE DIGITS ON DARK DRUMS -- black for the first five, red for the
three decimals. Most meters jomjol's networks were trained on are the
other way round, dark digits on white drums, with only the decimals
light-on-dark. Inverting the first five was measured on a real frame and
changed nothing, so it is not the thing to reach for first; sharpness
and levelling both mattered far more. Kept here because it is the
obvious suspect and someone will otherwise spend an evening on it.
If the red three ever misbehave while the black five are fine, give
those ROIs their own "model" -- each ROI may override the meter's.

_comment_photoaf: photoaf.jpg runs an autofocus pass and returns the full sensor.
shot.jpg returns the preview stream's last frame, which on this
phone is 720x480 and about 7 KB -- unreadable for eight drums.
_comment_prepare: Re-asserted before every shot, because IP Webcam forgets them when
the phone reboots or the app restarts -- and the failure that causes
is not an error, it is a quietly softer frame that misreads a drum
now and then.
All three were verified to stick: quality went 35 -> 90 and the
photo size is the full sensor. Read them back any time with
GET http://192.0.2.176:8080/status.json -> curvals.
FOCUS IS THE PROBLEM ON THIS PHONE. curvals.focusmode reads 'fixed'
and refuses every value -- macro, auto, continuous-picture,
continuous-video, edof and infinity were all tried and all silently
ignored. focus_distance is advertised by the app's own page but never
appears in curvals, so it is not real here either. The only control
that did anything is the bare /focus endpoint, which flips
curvals.focus to 'on'; that is why it is in this list and the
focusmode call is not.
A phone's fixed focus is usually hyperfocal -- sharp from about a
metre to infinity -- so a dial at 20 cm may simply be blurred. There
is a real tension: close enough that eight drums span 400+ px, far
enough that fixed focus is sharp. Shoot the meter and look before
assuming either. If it is soft, the cheap fixes in order are a clip-on
macro lens, then a different capture app that exposes Camera2 manual
focus, then going straight to the ESP32-CAM -- where focus is set by
unscrewing the lens and is therefore never in doubt.
_comment_pushed_camera: THE ESP32-CAM DOES NOT ANSWER, SO NOTHING HERE FETCHES FROM IT.
The node wakes, lights the meter, takes its frames, POSTs them to
/read and sleeps. There is no snapshot to pull: it is asleep, and it
is asleep because staying awake to be asked is what cooked the board.
So snapshot_url below is NOT how a reading happens any more. It is
only what /capture -- and therefore the /roi editor -- fetches when
somebody is drawing rectangles, and it points back at this service:
"snapshot_url": "http://127.0.0.1:8770/last.jpg?token=YOUR_TOKEN"
/last.jpg is the newest frame the node pushed, kept on disk as well
as in memory for exactly this: the editor has to work at a gas meter
with a laptop, hours after the last wake and possibly after a restart.
The token goes in the query string because a fetch made by this
service to itself sets no headers.
torch_on_url and prepare_urls are gone with the phone. The node
drives its own two LEDs, and its resolution, quality and exposure are
in firmware rather than in something that forgets them on reboot.
Focus is a lens that screws in and out -- which is what moving off
the phone bought, its fixed hyperfocal focus being the one fault no
config could reach.
A URL may still be an object -- {"url": ..., "method": "POST"} --
for anything that needs a POST to act. A bare string stays a GET.

_comment: Applied to every frame before anything else looks at it. Flip first,
then rotate. flip: none | horizontal | vertical | both.
rotate: 0 | 90 | 180 | 270, clockwise.
SET flip TO "horizontal" IF YOU USE THE FRONT CAMERA. A mirrored
frame breaks this twice: the digits are mirrored, and only 0, 1 and 8
survive that -- 2, 4, 6 and 9 become shapes the networks have never
seen and will guess at confidently. And the drum ORDER reverses, so
02246916 assembles as 61964220, with the carry rule running backwards
into the bargain.
Check rather than assume: some apps mirror the live preview but save
the still un-mirrored. Point the camera at anything with text on it,
open /capture, and read the text. If it reads normally, leave this
as "none".
rotate is here for the ESP32-CAM, which will very likely end up on a
bracket that is not the right way up.
deskew is fine levelling in degrees, positive counter-clockwise, and
it matters more than it sounds. Every ROI is an axis-aligned
rectangle, so a tilted row of drums cannot be fitted by any set of
them. Worse, the model reads a digit's HEIGHT in its box as PHASE --
a digit sitting low reads as "not yet arrived". The first real frame
off this meter ran about 3.5 degrees out of level and came back
uniformly 0.2-0.4 low on all eight drums, which looks like a broken
model and is really just a crooked photograph. Level it here, THEN
draw the boxes.

_comment_quality: QUALITY, as opposed to possibility. min_matches above only asks
whether a transform could be computed at all; these four ask whether
to believe the one that came back.
Measured on this meter, 2026-09-05: a frame matched on 21 inliers of
147 matches and warped 808 px, reported ok=true, and was read
confidently off the wrong part of the dial. Every later guard passed
it -- the digits were sharp and the number plausible, because the
ROIs had landed on a different part of a real photograph of a real
meter.
That is the failure worth naming. A blank or blurred frame is caught
everywhere: by confidence, by the zero rule, by the rate limit. A
frame aligned to the WRONG PLACE is sharp, confident and stable, and
reading it five times reproduces it five times. Alignment quality is
the only signal that sees it.
min_inlier_ratio is the primary bar. A genuine match on this meter
runs ~1000 inliers; the bad frame ran 21 of 147, a ratio of 0.14.
Real matches agree in bulk, bogus ones agree by accident.
min_inliers is a floor that makes the ratio mean something -- 2 of 2
is a ratio of 1.0 and means nothing at all.
max_shift_px is deliberately generous, because CORRECTING drift is
what alignment is for and a tight bound would defeat it. 300 px is
12% of the frame; the largest correction verified as working here
was 120 px with 2 degrees. It is not here to police movement, only
to refuse a match no camera on a bracket could have produced.
Any of them may be null to switch that bar off.
_comment: THE MOST IMPORTANT BLOCK IN THIS FILE. Every ROI is a fixed pixel
rectangle, so without alignment the coordinates are only valid until
the camera moves -- and it moves. Measured here: the phone drifted 26
px down between drawing the boxes and the next session, which turned
a perfect 8/8 read into gibberish that looked exactly like a broken
model. It cost four debugging sessions.
auto_reference true means the first frame read becomes the reference
automatically, so this protects you without anyone remembering a
button. That is safe because the frame being read IS the frame the
ROIs are drawn against, which is the coordinate space they live in.
ORB then warps every later frame back onto it. Verified on this very
meter, blur and all: a 26 px shift came back to 0.1 px, and 120 px
with 2 degrees of rotation to under 1 px, on ~1000 inliers.
MOVE THE CAMERA OR REDRAW THE BOXES AND YOU MUST REPLACE THE
REFERENCE -- POST /reference, or the button in /roi. The ROIs and the
reference are one matched pair.
'reject' on failure because reading fixed rectangles out of a frame
nothing has corrected produces a confident wrong number, which is
worse than no number at all.
Even out the light on a drum before the network sees it.
OFF BY DEFAULT, and that is a measurement problem rather than
caution. dig-class100 was trained on ordinary colour crops; every
mode here trades that distribution for contrast, and which way the
trade lands is decided by frames, not by argument. Run
tools/score.py --preprocess against a labelled corpus and turn on
whichever wins. There is no corpus yet, so there is no answer yet.
none          leave the pixels alone
clahe         CLAHE on L in LAB -- only lightness moves, the hues
the network knows survive. Try this one first: it
fixes a drum dimmed by a light off to one side and
it is the mildest thing here.
green         keep green, drop red and blue. White ink has green
in it, red has almost none, so the three
white-on-red decimals come out as white strokes on
near-black instead of white on mid-red. On the five
black-on-white drums it is close to greyscale and
costs little.
clahe+green   both, in that order.
SETTABLE PER ROI as well, and this dial is the reason: five drums
black on white, three white on red. They are different pictures and
they need not have the same answer. Put "preprocess" on the ROI to
override this block for one drum -- the same argument "model"
makes, for the same reason.
WHAT NONE OF IT CAN DO is recover a blown highlight. A flash
reflected off the meter glass saturates the sensor and a saturated
pixel has nothing left to stretch. That is fixed by moving the
light, which is what two LEDs off to the sides are for.
Read the dial several times and require the readings to agree.
TWO, not five. The camera pushes its frames now: it wakes, lights
the meter, shoots and sleeps, and every extra frame is time with
two LEDs on and a radio up on a board that overheats. Two frames
still kill the whole random-error class -- a flicker or a drum
caught mid-tick has to happen twice, identically, to survive --
and the fifth frame was never buying much over the second.
When the camera pushes, this number is not even consulted: the
node sends what it sends and every frame of it is read.
One frame can be wrong in ways that leave no trace in the number: a
flicker, sensor noise, a drum caught mid-tick. None of those repeat,
so demanding agreement across a burst removes the whole class.
WHAT IT CANNOT DO, and this matters more than what it can: sampling
catches RANDOM error and is blind to SYSTEMATIC error. Misplaced
ROIs read the same wrong number off every frame, unanimously and
confidently. Agreeing samples are not verification. The align
block above is what stands against that, and tools/score.py against
a labelled corpus is the only thing that proves either.
gap_ms is short on purpose -- long enough to decorrelate sensor
noise between frames, short enough that the last drum is unlikely to
move. A long gap only invites the disagreement this is detecting.
max_last_digit_step allows the last PUBLISHED drum to advance
during the burst -- samples are compared after report_decimals has
trimmed them, so the step here is 0.01 and not the dial's 0.001.
It can only go UP: a sample lower than the one before it is a
misread however small, and is always refused. Set 0 to demand
identical readings, which refuses a real tick roughly one burst in
twenty.
One step per ~10 s burst is a flow ceiling of 3.6 m3/h. If reads are
refused for spread while the boiler is on, that is what was hit --
raise this to 2 rather than suspecting the model.
COST: five samples is five captures. With a torch configured that is
five on/off cycles and five settles, so a read takes seconds rather
than a second. Set timeout: 30 on the Home Assistant rest_command --
its default of 10 is not enough.
samples: 1 disables confirmation. POST /read takes that path anyway,
having been handed a single frame, and says so with an `unconfirmed`
field rather than implying a check that never ran.

_comment_report_decimals: The dial has 3 decimal drums; only 2 of them reach Home Assistant.
All 8 are still read, drawn on the annotated frame and scored -- the
0.001 drum is dropped from the VALUE, not from the reading.
Why: that drum turns continuously, roughly once every two minutes at
this house's idle burn and once every 1.8 seconds with the boiler
firing. A confirmation burst is five frames at ~1.84 s plus gaps, so
about ten seconds, and max_last_digit_step allows ONE step across it.
Published to 0.001 that is a flow ceiling of 0.36 m3/h -- barely above
the pilot flame -- so every read taken while the boiler ran disagreed
with itself and was refused. The meter went blind exactly when there
was something to see. At 0.01 the same budget permits 3.6 m3/h, above
anything this house burns and below the meter's Qmax of 6.
It also stopped that drum's jitter from vetoing good frames: at idle
the true advance between five-minute polls is about two steps of
0.001, the same size as the drum's own read noise, and tolerance_down
is 0.0, so noise alone could read as a decrease.
WHY NOT 1 OR 0 DECIMALS, which is the tempting next step. max_delta
is 0.6 m3 per 5 min, just above this meter's physical maximum of 0.5.
A published value quantized to R makes a legitimate advance look up to
R larger, so max_delta must be at least 0.5 + R. At whole cubic metres
that is 1.6 -- and a misread UNITS drum is exactly +1 m3, which would
then sit inside the allowance and pass unnoticed. The rate limit is
one of only two guards that catch a confident misread (see gate); at
0.01 it keeps its 0.6 and keeps catching that one. Do not coarsen this
past 2 without raising max_delta and understanding what it stops
catching.
Cost, for completeness: the published total is always within 0.01 m3
of the dial. It does NOT accumulate -- each reading is an absolute
total, not a sum of deltas -- and 0.01 m3 is under 0.1 kWh.
_comment_counter: How the drums are geared. THIS METER IS "jump" and it is not a detail
-- the wrong value corrupts digits the model read correctly.
jump: each whole-number drum stays put until the drum to its right
completes a revolution, then snaps forward. Every drum shows a digit
squarely in its window, so round each one independently and let no
continuous: every drum geared to its neighbour, common on water meters.
At 9.5 on the units drum the tens drum is already 95% of the way to its
next digit and looks like it, so each drum has to be resolved against
Read it off a photograph: this meter stood at 02246.916 -- decimals
91.6% through -- while the units drum showed a clean centred 6. Geared
continuously it would have been at 6.916, showing mostly the 7 behind
it. It was not, so it jumps.
Measured cost of getting it wrong here: the model returned
true reading. The continuous carry rule turned that into 02235905 --
four digits wrong at 100% model confidence, including a perfect 4.0

_comment: max_delta 0.6 m3 per 5 minutes is deliberately generous: this house
burns about 0.028 m3/h, and even a G4 meter at its rated maximum of
6 m3/h only reaches 0.5 m3 in five minutes. It is there to catch a
misread digit, not to police the boiler.
tolerance_down 0.0 -- the sensor is total_increasing and a decrease
of more than 10% is taken as a meter reset that retyping does not
undo. Never accept one.
require_prevalue refuses a reading taken with nothing to compare
against. Without a previous value there is no rate limit and no
decrease check -- the two guards that actually catch a misread, and
the only two that do not ask the model's opinion. Measured
2026-09-05: a blank grey wall reads as 0 at 0.992 confidence and
black reads 11111111 at 0.775, so confidence is the guard least able
to carry this on its own.
Accepting an unguarded reading would make the first poll after a
Home Assistant restart the least protected of the day -- precisely
when a wrong value sets a total_increasing sensor's statistics
baseline, permanently. The cost of refusing is one poll:
input_number restores its last value, so prevalue is populated on
every poll after that.
min_confidence_last_digit is null because the last drum turns
continuously and is legitimately mid-transition most of the time.
Holding it to the same bar as the others rejects good frames all day.
Since report_decimals it is also the drum that no longer reaches the
value, so its confidence cannot change the number anyway. The two
line up by coincidence, not by derivation -- min_confidence polices
every drum EXCEPT the last one positionally. Drop a second drum from
the value and the 0.01 drum would still be policed here while no
longer being published, which is a refusal for nothing.
